title: Missing type for PEP695 `TypeAliasType` vs `TypeAlias` when using `TypeAdapter`

judge.reasoning: The issue is that `TypeAdapter(my_type)` on a PEP 695 alias gives the wrong type, `TypeAliasType`; the user expects the aliased type, `list[dict[str, list[int]]]`. Patch A fixes the root cause. It replaces the `type[T]`/`Any` overload pair on `TypeAdapter.__init__` with one `type: TypeForm[T]` signature (PEP 747). Under PEP 747 a PEP 695 alias is a valid type expression, so a supporting checker can infer `T` as the aliased type. The same change fixes the related cases (`Annotated[...]`, `int | str`, `Union[...]`), and its updated typechecking tests now assert those cases directly instead of suppressing assert-type failures. That shows the previously broken inference now works. Patch A has drawbacks. It is very broad: TypeForm is applied across fields, serializers, `create_model` and the pipeline, and it adds Pyrefly config, CI pinning and many `pyrefly: ignore` comments. It removes the fallback overloads, so checkers without TypeForm support may regress. It also does not add a test that uses a PEP 695/`TypeAliasType` alias specifically. Patch B is a narrower mitigation. It adds an overload that matches `TypeAliasType` first and returns `TypeAdapter[Any]`. This stops the wrong `TypeAliasType` inference, but it still does not produce the type the issue asks for; users must annotate manually. Its tests are targeted and correct but only confirm the `Any` fallback. On correctness, which is weighted first, Patch A actually delivers the expected inference, while Patch B hides the symptom by downgrading to `Any`. Patch A's extra churn adds some risk but does not outweigh this.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

There seems to be a difference between the type that is returned from TypeAdapter when used on a PEP695 `TypeAliasType` compared to when it is used on a `TypeAlias`. See example below. When `TypeAdapter` is used on a `TypeAlias`, the correct type is shown. However, when the `TypeAliasType` is used, the type is shown as `TypeAliasType`. This causes the type-checker to see red. 

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import TypeAlias, reveal_type

from pydantic import TypeAdapter

my_type_alias: TypeAlias = list[dict[str, list[int]]]
x: my_type_alias = [{"a": [1, 2, 3]}]

res = TypeAdapter(type=my_type_alias).validate_python(x)
reveal_type(res)  # type of res is "list[dict[str, list[int]]]"


type my_type = list[dict[str, list[int]]]
x: my_type = [{"a": [1, 2, 3]}]

res = TypeAdapter(type=my_type).validate_python(x)
reveal_type(res)  # type of res is "TypeAliasType"
```


### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.6.3
        pydantic-core version: 2.16.3
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=true
                 install path: /usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/pydantic
               python version: 3.12.2 (main, Feb 13 2024, 09:17:46) [GCC 12.2.0]
                     platform: Linux-5.15.133.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.36
             related packages: pyright-1.1.352 pyright-1.1.353 typing_extensions-4.10.0 pydantic-extra-types-2.6.0 fastapi-0.110.0 pydantic-settings-2.2.1
                       commit: unknown
```

title: Mypy internal error when subclassing a generic model with a recursive type variable

judge.reasoning:
The two code fixes are functionally the same. Each imports `has_placeholder` from `mypy.semanal_shared`. When any collected field type still contains a placeholder, each calls `self._api.defer()` (unless on the final iteration) and returns False. This stops the plugin from serializing an unresolved PlaceholderType into metadata, which is the root cause of the AssertionError. Patch A puts the check in the existing `field.type is None` condition; Patch B adds a separate branch. That is a cosmetic difference, and both comments explain the reason clearly. On correctness and scope they are tied.

Tests are where they differ. Patch A appends a reproduction to the existing `generics.py` module. It only checks that mypy no longer crashes and that `child.children` is `list[Child]`. It also uses a string bound (`bound='Element'`), which is slightly different from the issue's `bound=Element`, and has an odd placeholder docstring (`"""<link>"""`). Patch B adds a dedicated `recursive_generic_model.py` module, registers it in `test_mypy.py` under the strict plugin config, and commits the expected output file. Its scenario is broader: the exact pattern from the issue, a second field (`Optional[ElementT]`), a further subclass (`GrandChild`) inheriting the resolved fields, and negative cases. Those negative cases check that the synthesized `__init__` really carries the resolved `Child` types, by expecting `list-item` and `arg-type` errors when `Other` is passed. That confirms the deferred pass produces correct signatures, not just the absence of a crash. Patch B's test coverage is clearly more thorough and more meaningful, so B wins.

title: Cannot use model_dump(include=...) with @model_serializer (raises PydanticOmit)

judge.reasoning:
Patch B fixes the root cause. A `SerializationInfo` passed as the second argument to the wrap handler was being used as a filter key, which caused `PydanticOmit` when `include` was set. Patch B now treats it as if no index key was given. As a result, the issue's exact example (`handler(self, info)` with `include={'bar'}`) works and returns the expected filtered output. Its tests would fail before the change and pass after it. They cover the core-level wrap serializer, `model_serializer`, and `field_serializer`, across include and exclude and both python and json modes. It also updates the `SerializerFunctionWrapHandler` protocol type to match the accepted usage.

Patch A does not make the issue's code work. It only swaps the confusing `PydanticOmit` for a `TypeError`. Its type check runs whenever an `index_key` is supplied, before any filter lookup. So `handler(value, info)` would now raise even when no `include`/`exclude` is given. That breaks a pattern that previously worked and that pydantic's own `WrapSerializer` docstring used; Patch A has to rewrite that docstring example, which confirms the breakage. Its single test only checks the new error message for an odd `bytes` key and does not exercise the reported scenario.

On correctness, regression risk and test relevance, Patch B is clearly better.

title: Some Field attributes lost in JSON schema when using RootModel

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the issue in the same place, `GenerateJsonSchema._update_class_schema`. Each one reads the RootModel's `root` FieldInfo and emits `examples` (via `to_jsonable_python`), `deprecated: True`, and the root field's title. Both let an explicit `config['title']` take precedence over the field title.

Correctness differences are minor:
- **Title precedence:** Patch A puts the root field title ahead of `model_title_generator`. Patch B applies it only when neither config title nor generator set one. An explicit field title is arguably more specific than a generic generator, so A's ordering is reasonable, but neither choice is clearly wrong.
- **Examples:** Patch A overwrites `examples`, while Patch B uses `setdefault`. The inner schema rarely has its own examples here, so this is roughly equivalent.
- **Deprecated:** Patch A checks `is not None and is not False`, which handles deprecation-message strings and `deprecated` instances. Patch B uses truthiness, which is equivalent except for an empty-string message.
- **Description:** Patch A also refactors the existing description branch to reuse the cached `root_field_info`. This is a small clarity improvement with no added risk.

Tests are the main differentiator. Both cover examples, deprecated, title, and config-title override. Patch A goes further:
- It checks that a non-JSON-native example (a `date`) is serialized to `'2020-01-02'`, exercising the `to_jsonable_python` path.
- It checks that a string deprecation message yields `deprecated: True`.
- It checks the nested-in-model case, where the RootModel appears under `$defs` with the title and examples intact. This is the realistic usage scenario.

Patch B's tests are narrower and miss these paths. Overall the fixes are equivalent in substance, and A has stronger test coverage and slightly cleaner code.

title: mypy `[arg-type]`-error when passing in type that can be converted to `RootModel`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same core fix. They register `_RootModelMetaclass` with the metaclass hook so the plugin, not dataclass_transform, governs RootModel subclasses. They also stop the plugin from deferring to the hand-written typed `__init__` on `RootModel` itself, which is the root cause of `RootModel[float]('1.0')` erroring when `init_typed` is off.

Patch A removes the skip guard when the class is `RootModel`. The generic `add_initializer` path then regenerates `RootModel.__init__` through field collection on a class whose root type is a TypeVar. That probably works, but it is implicit and also replaces the declared signature in typed mode.

Patch B handles `RootModel` explicitly. It leaves the declared typed `__init__` alone when `init_typed` is true. When it is false, it installs a clear `root: Any = ..., **data: Any` signature that mirrors the runtime. This is a narrower, more predictable change.

On tests, Patch B is clearly stronger. It covers:
- the alias case
- direct `RootModel[float](...)` calls
- keyword `root=` usage
- Optional root types
- dict roots with `**data`
- subclasses
- `assert_type` checks that the root type is preserved
- a strict (`init_typed`) config, confirming that typed mode still reports errors

Patch A tests only the positional alias and subclass cases under the default and plugin configs.

Patch B also makes `root` positional-required when it has no default. That is extra scope and slightly risky, but it matches runtime behavior (validation fails without `root`) and is covered by tests. Overall, B's explicit handling and broader verification make it the better fix.

title: Decimal JSON schema pattern uses lookahead regex unsupported by pydantic-core

judge.reasoning: Patch B fixes the root cause directly. It rewrites the decimal pattern generator so no look-around assertions are emitted, and it keeps the existing behavior of including a `pattern` describing `max_digits`/`decimal_places`. It also handles pattern size: above `_DECIMAL_PATTERN_MAX_DIGITS_LIMIT`, it falls back to checking integer and fractional digits separately, so the regex stays within pydantic-core's limits. Its new tests match the issue's scenario: they feed the emitted pattern back through `TypeAdapter(Annotated[str, StringConstraints(pattern=...)])`, including large `max_digits` values (51, 300). They also check accept/reject behavior for a model in both validation and serialization modes. These tests would fail before the change. Patch A changes default behavior instead: it drops the `pattern` from Decimal JSON schemas entirely and adds an opt-in `get_decimal_pattern`/`build_decimal_pattern` hook backed by a much larger new regex builder (exponents, inf/nan, a separate serialization grammar). That does make the issue's symptom go away. However, it is a user-visible behavior change and a broad redesign well beyond the ask. Its new builder is never tested by compiling it in pydantic-core, which is the exact failure the issue reports; it only tests with Python's `re`. Its docs also contain two consecutive `version-changed` blocks that contradict each other: one says the pattern is included, the next says it no longer is. B is the more focused, behavior-preserving fix, with tests that exercise the reported failure.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

  Pydantic v2 emits a JSON schema for Decimal fields that includes a regex pattern with a negative lookahead `((?!...))`. This pattern cannot be compiled by `pydantic-core`'s Rust regex crate, which does not support look-around assertions.

  This means the JSON schema pydantic produces for Decimal cannot be round-tripped back through pydantic's own validation  e.g. constructing a `TypeAdapter` with `StringConstraints(pattern=...)` using the emitted pattern fails with a `SchemaError`.

  This is a practical problem for any tooling that reconstructs pydantic types from emitted JSON schemas (e.g. MCP structured content parsing via FastMCP).


### Example Code

```Python
"""Minimal reproduction: Decimal JSON schema pattern uses lookahead unsupported by pydantic-core.

Pydantic generates a JSON schema for Decimal fields with a regex pattern that uses
a negative lookahead (?!...). When that schema is round-tripped back through pydantic
(e.g. via TypeAdapter with StringConstraints), pydantic-core's Rust regex engine
rejects it because it does not support look-around assertions.
"""

from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, StringConstraints, TypeAdapter


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    amount: Decimal


def test_decimal_json_schema_pattern_roundtrips_through_pydantic_core():
    schema = MyModel.model_json_schema()

    # Decimal emits an anyOf with a string variant carrying the pattern
    string_variant = next(v for v in schema['properties']['amount']['anyOf'] if v.get('type') == 'string')
    pattern = string_variant['pattern']

    # The emitted pattern contains a negative lookahead:
    assert '(?!' in pattern

    # Feeding it back into StringConstraints fails with:
    #   SchemaError: regex parse error: look-around ... is not supported
    ConstrainedStr = Annotated[str, StringConstraints(pattern=pattern)]
    TypeAdapter(ConstrainedStr)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    test_decimal_json_schema_pattern_roundtrips_through_pydantic_core()
```

```Text

+def _repeat(atom: str, min_count: int, max_count: int) -> str:
+    """Build a regex repetition of `atom` between `min_count` and `max_count` times (inclusive), using the shortest quantifier."""
+    if min_count > max_count or max_count == 0:
+        return ''
+    if min_count == max_count:
+        return atom if min_count == 1 else f'{atom}{{{min_count}}}'
+    if (min_count, max_count) == (0, 1):
+        return f'{atom}?'
+    return f'{atom}{{{min_count},{max_count}}}'

+    """Build a regex matching the integers between 1 and `max_value` (inclusive), without leading zeros."""
+    digits = str(max_value)
+    length = len(digits)
+    alts: list[str] = [f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", k - 1, k - 1)}' for k in range(1, length)]
+    for i, char in enumerate(digits):
+        d = int(char)
+        low = 1 if i == 0 else 0
+        high = d if i == length - 1 else d - 1

+            alts.append(f'{digits[:i]}{char_class}{_repeat("[0-9]", length - i - 1, length - i - 1)}')

+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'{int_part}(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'{opt_int_part}{frac_part}']
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}' if max_digits else '0+'
+        alts.append(rf'{int_part}(?:\.0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            rf'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", whole, whole)}\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits - whole)}0*'
+            for whole in range(max_digits)
+        ] or [r'0*\.0+']
+    else:
+        assert decimal_places is not None
+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, decimal_places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, decimal_places)}0*' if decimal_places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'[0-9]+(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'[0-9]*{frac_part}']
+
+    alts.append(f'{number}{exponent}')
+    return rf'^[+-]?(?:{"|".join(alts)}{non_finite})$'
+
+
+def _decimal_serialization_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:
+    """Build the decimal pattern for the `'serialization'` mode.
+
+    Decimals are serialized using `str()`, producing either:
+
+    - The plain notation (`'123.45'`), when the exponent is lower than or equal to 0 and the adjusted
+      exponent is greater than or equal to -6.
+    - The scientific notation otherwise (`'1E+3'`, `'1.5E-7'`, `'0E-10'`), with a single digit before
+      the optional decimal point and an always signed exponent.
+
+    Trailing zeros of the decimal part are preserved by `str()`, but aren't counted by the validation logic.
+    """
+
+    def frac_part(places: int) -> str:
+        return rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+
+    # Plain notation:
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'(?:0|[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole - 1)})' if whole else '0'
+        alts.append(f'{int_part}(?:{frac_part(places)})?')
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        alts.append(rf'0(?:\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", whole - 1, whole - 1)}(?:{frac_part(max_digits - whole)})?'
+            for whole in range(1, max_digits + 1)
+        ]
+    elif decimal_places is not None:
+        alts.append(f'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:{frac_part(decimal_places)})?')
+    else:
+        alts.append(r'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:\.[0-9]+)?')
+
+    # Zero with an exponent (e.g. `'0E-10'`), which normalizes to zero and thus satisfies any constraint:
+    alts.append(r'0E[+-][1-9][0-9]*')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a positive exponent `k` (e.g. `'1.5E+3'`): the value has `k + 1` whole digits
+    # and no decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_exponent = max_digits - (decimal_places or 0) - 1
+        if max_exponent >= 1:
+            alts.append(rf'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+{_int_range_pattern(max_exponent)}')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a negative exponent `k` (`k >= 7`, e.g. `'1.5E-7'`): the value has no whole digits,
+    # and `k` + (the number of significant decimal digits of the coefficient) decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E-[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_places = min(c for c in (max_digits, decimal_places) if c is not None)
+        alts += [f'[1-9](?:{frac_part(max_places - k)})?E-{k}' for k in range(7, max_places + 1)]
+
+    if allow_inf_nan:
+        # `str()` produces `'Infinity'`, `'NaN'` and `'sNaN'` (with an optional payload):
+        alts += ['Infinity', 's?NaN[0-9]*']
+
+    return rf'^-?(?:{"|".join(alts)})$'
 
 
 def _deduplicate_schemas(schemas: Iterable[JsonDict]) -> list[JsonDict]:
     return list({_make_json_hashable(schema): schema for schema in schemas}.values())
 
 
+_HashableJsonValue: TypeAlias = (
+    int | float | str | bool | None | tuple['_HashableJsonValue', ...] | tuple[tuple[str, '_HashableJsonValue'], ...]
+)
+
+
 def _make_json_hashable(value: JsonValue) -> _HashableJsonValue:
     if isinstance(value, dict):
         return tuple(sorted((k, _make_json_hashable(v)) for k, v in value.items()))

title: Decimal JSON schema pattern rejects pydantic's own scientific notation serialization output (v2.12 regression)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches stop the reported value '1E-7' from failing the schema. They differ in how completely they close the underlying problem: a schema pattern that rejects pydantic's own serialized output.

Patch A appends an alternation, `|^[+-]?(?=\.?\d)\d*\.?\d*[eE][+-]?\d+$`, to every decimal pattern. This directly implements the fix the issue suggests, and its tests check that `model_dump_json` output matches the serialization pattern. However, it leaves other cases of the same mismatch in place. With `allow_inf_nan`, pydantic serializes values as 'Infinity' or 'NaN', and A's pattern still rejects those. A also keeps the lookahead-based pattern, which the issue implies causes trouble for downstream tooling, and it does not touch the pre-existing anchoring quirks in the constrained branches.

Patch B goes back to the v2.11 behaviour: by default, decimal schemas get no `pattern`. That removes the regression at its source, so no serialized value (scientific notation, Infinity or NaN) can be rejected. B moves pattern generation into overridable `get_decimal_pattern` and `build_decimal_pattern` methods. It also adds an opt-in builder whose serialization pattern describes exactly what `str(Decimal)` produces, including exponents, constraints and inf/nan. That builder has no lookaheads and uses portable `[0-9]`.

B's tests are much stronger. They round-trip values through `dump_json` and check them against the pattern across many constraint combinations, and they also check rejection cases and inf/nan handling.

B is a broader redesign, which adds code surface and some risk. That risk is contained because the complex builder is opt-in and the default path is trivially safe. B's docs are slightly awkward, with two version-changed blocks.

On balance, B fixes the regression more completely and robustly, with better test evidence, so it is the better fix.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

**`model_json_schema(mode="serialization")` pattern for `Decimal` breaks on scientific notation**

The serialization schema for `Decimal` fields generates a regex that rejects values that `model_dump_json()` itself produces.

Specifically: `pydantic-core`'s serializer calls `str()` on `Decimal` objects, which outputs scientific notation for small/large values. E.g. `Decimal('0.0000001')` becomes `"1E-7"`. But the pattern added in #11987 (`^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\d*\.?\d*$`) has no `[eE]` component, so it'll never match those strings.

As a result, any downstream consumer validating `model_dump_json()` output against `model_json_schema()`, such as OpenAPI validators and codegen + validation tools like Orval + Zod, will intermittently reject perfectly valid serialized values. Intermittent because only certain `Decimal` values trigger scientific notation.

**v2.11**:
```json
{"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}
```

**v2.12**:
```json
{"anyOf": [{"pattern": "^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\\d*\\.?\\d*$", "type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}
```

Two possible fixes:
- Append `(?:[eE][+-]?\d+)?` to the pattern in serialization mode
- Normalize `Decimal` to fixed-point during serialization before it ever hits the schema

### Example Code

```Python
import json
import re
from decimal import Decimal
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyModel(BaseModel):

+        return ''
+    if min_count == max_count:
+        return atom if min_count == 1 else f'{atom}{{{min_count}}}'
+    if (min_count, max_count) == (0, 1):
+        return f'{atom}?'
+    return f'{atom}{{{min_count},{max_count}}}'
+
+
+def _int_range_pattern(max_value: int) -> str:
+    """Build a regex matching the integers between 1 and `max_value` (inclusive), without leading zeros."""
+    digits = str(max_value)
+    length = len(digits)
+    alts: list[str] = [f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", k - 1, k - 1)}' for k in range(1, length)]
+    for i, char in enumerate(digits):
+        d = int(char)
+        low = 1 if i == 0 else 0
+        high = d if i == length - 1 else d - 1
+        if high >= low:
+            char_class = str(low) if low == high else f'[{low}-{high}]'
+            alts.append(f'{digits[:i]}{char_class}{_repeat("[0-9]", length - i - 1, length - i - 1)}')
+    return alts[0] if len(alts) == 1 else f'(?:{"|".join(alts)})'
+
+
+def _decimal_validation_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:
+    """Build the decimal pattern for the `'validation'` mode."""
+
+    number = r'(?:[0-9]+\.?[0-9]*|\.[0-9]+)'  # e.g. 1, 1., .5
+    exponent = r'[eE][+-]?[0-9]+'  # e.g. e5, E5, e-7
+    # e.g. Infinity, inf, NaN, sNaN, NaN123 (case-insensitive). Spelled out explicitly, as inline flags
+    # aren't supported by all regular expression engines:
+    non_finite = r'|[iI][nN][fF](?:[iI][nN][iI][tT][yY])?|[sS]?[nN][aA][nN][0-9]*' if allow_inf_nan else ''
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        return rf'^[+-]?(?:{number}(?:{exponent})?{non_finite})$'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        # If `decimal_places > max_digits`, no whole digits are allowed and `max_digits` bounds the decimal places:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, whole)}' if whole else '0+'
+        opt_int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole)}'
+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'{int_part}(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'{opt_int_part}{frac_part}']
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}' if max_digits else '0+'
+        alts.append(rf'{int_part}(?:\.0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            rf'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", whole, whole)}\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits - whole)}0*'
+            for whole in range(max_digits)
+        ] or [r'0*\.0+']
+    else:
+        assert decimal_places is not None
+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, decimal_places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, decimal_places)}0*' if decimal_places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'[0-9]+(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'[0-9]*{frac_part}']
+
+    alts.append(f'{number}{exponent}')
+    return rf'^[+-]?(?:{"|".join(alts)}{non_finite})$'
+
+
+def _decimal_serialization_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:
+    """Build the decimal pattern for the `'serialization'` mode.
+
+    Decimals are serialized using `str()`, producing either:
+
+    - The plain notation (`'123.45'`), when the exponent is lower than or equal to 0 and the adjusted
+      exponent is greater than or equal to -6.
+    - The scientific notation otherwise (`'1E+3'`, `'1.5E-7'`, `'0E-10'`), with a single digit before
+      the optional decimal point and an always signed exponent.
+
+    Trailing zeros of the decimal part are preserved by `str()`, but aren't counted by the validation logic.
+    """
+
+    def frac_part(places: int) -> str:
+        return rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+
+    # Plain notation:
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'(?:0|[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole - 1)})' if whole else '0'
+        alts.append(f'{int_part}(?:{frac_part(places)})?')
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        alts.append(rf'0(?:\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", whole - 1, whole - 1)}(?:{frac_part(max_digits - whole)})?'
+            for whole in range(1, max_digits + 1)
+        ]
+    elif decimal_places is not None:
+        alts.append(f'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:{frac_part(decimal_places)})?')
+    else:
+        alts.append(r'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:\.[0-9]+)?')
+
+    # Zero with an exponent (e.g. `'0E-10'`), which normalizes to zero and thus satisfies any constraint:
+    alts.append(r'0E[+-][1-9][0-9]*')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a positive exponent `k` (e.g. `'1.5E+3'`): the value has `k + 1` whole digits
+    # and no decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_exponent = max_digits - (decimal_places or 0) - 1
+        if max_exponent >= 1:
+            alts.append(rf'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+{_int_range_pattern(max_exponent)}')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a negative exponent `k` (`k >= 7`, e.g. `'1.5E-7'`): the value has no whole digits,
+    # and `k` + (the number of significant decimal digits of the coefficient) decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E-[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_places = min(c for c in (max_digits, decimal_places) if c is not None)
+        alts += [f'[1-9](?:{frac_part(max_places - k)})?E-{k}' for k in range(7, max_places + 1)]
+
+    if allow_inf_nan:
+        # `str()` produces `'Infinity'`, `'NaN'` and `'sNaN'` (with an optional payload):
+        alts += ['Infinity', 's?NaN[0-9]*']
+
+    return rf'^-?(?:{"|".join(alts)})$'

Patch A fixes the reported problem directly. It changes `BaseModel.__class_getitem__`'s `typevar_values` annotation from `type[Any] | tuple[type[Any], ...]` to `Any`. Every type checker, including PyCharm, which the issue names, will then accept `None`, `Literal[...]`, `Optional[...]` and other special forms as type arguments. Its tests are on point: a runtime test parametrizes a generic model with `None`, `Literal[1]` and `Optional[int]` and checks validation behaviour. It also adds pyright/mypy typechecking cases for `GenericModel[None]`, `GenericModel[Literal[1]]` and `RootModel[None]`, which exercise exactly the scenario in the issue. The assertion on the annotation string is a little brittle, but harmless.

Patch B tackles the issue as part of a broad PEP 747 `TypeForm` migration. It does annotate `__class_getitem__` with `TypeForm[Any] | tuple[TypeForm[Any], ...]`, which in principle accepts `None`. However, it adds no test for the issue's scenario (parametrizing a generic `BaseModel` with `None`). Its tests cover `TypeAdapter`, `create_model`, `ValidateAs` and pyrefly ignore comments instead. It also brings significant risk and unrelated churn:
- It removes the `TypeAdapter.__init__` overloads, including the `Any` fallback. This depends on every type checker supporting `TypeForm`; its own tests show mypy and pyrefly don't handle sentinels.
- It adds `# pyright: ignore` suppressions on `PydanticUndefined` defaults.
- It changes `FieldInfo`/`create_model` public signatures.
- It pins the pyright version in CI, adds a pyrefly config, and touches the Makefile.
- It edits many typechecking test files only to add pyrefly ignore comments.

Tools without `TypeForm` support, such as PyCharm, may still reject `Box[None]` under Patch B, so it may not even resolve the reported symptom. Patch A is correct, minimal, and well tested for the issue.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Pydantic's BaseModel.__class_getitem__ is annotated as `typevar_values: type[Any] | tuple[type[Any], ...]`, which causes type checkers to reject `None` as a type argument even though `None` is a valid PEP 484 type
annotation meaning `type(None)` / `NoneType`.

Error in PyCharm: `Expected type 'type | tuple[type, ...]', got 'type[None]'`

Root cause: pydantic/main.py BaseModel.__class_getitem__ signature should accept
`None` (and other special forms) as valid type arguments, not just `type[Any]`.

We could use `NoneType` to get rid of the problem, however, I suggest we update annotation on pydantic side.

### Example Code

```Python
import pydantic as p


class Box[T](p.BaseModel):
    pass


# Triggers the warning because Pydantic's __class_getitem__ is typed as
# typevar_values: type[Any] | tuple[type[Any], ...]
# and None is not type[Any]:
x = Box[None]()
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.12.5
        pydantic-core version: 2.41.5
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.12.1 (main, Jan 29 2024, 11:55:01) [Clang 15.0.0 (clang-1500.1.0.2.5)]
                     platform: macOS-26.4.1-arm64-arm-64bit
             related packages: pydantic-settings-2.13.1 typing_extensions-4.15.0
                       commit: unknown
```

title: RootModel.model_dump() typing signature rejects supported serialization arguments

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same core fix to the TYPE_CHECKING-only `RootModel.model_dump()` signature: `context` widened to `Any | None`, `fallback` and `polymorphic_serialization` added in the base-method order, and `include`/`exclude` tightened to `IncEx | None`. Either one resolves the root cause.

Tests are where they differ. Patch A puts regression cases in `tests/typechecking/root_model.py`, which is the location the issue proposes. The mypy, pyright and pyrefly suites run that file, and those `assert_type` calls would fail type checking before the fix. A also adds a runtime test confirming the three calls actually work and produce the expected output.

Patch B's test is a fragile hack. It sets the global `typing.TYPE_CHECKING = True` and re-executes `root_model.py` as a second module. That rebuilds the metaclass and dataclass_transform machinery and briefly mutates global interpreter state. It then compares stringified annotations and demands that the docstrings match exactly. This catches drift in an unusual way, but it is brittle and not how the repo's type-checking tests are written.

To satisfy that docstring-equality assertion, B also replaces the RootModel-specific docstring with a copy of BaseModel's. The copy includes "Returns: A dictionary representation of the model", which is inaccurate for RootModel. B moves the original explanation into a comment, which is churn that obscures the fix. B also moves the `Callable` import out of the TYPE_CHECKING block to runtime for no reason.

Patch A's change is minimal, matches conventions, and is tested in the right place.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`RootModel` inherits the runtime implementation of `BaseModel.model_dump()`, but defines a separate declaration under `TYPE_CHECKING` to preserve its more precise return type.

That declaration has diverged from the base method:

- `context` is restricted to `dict[str, Any] | None` instead of `Any | None`.
- `fallback` is missing.
- `polymorphic_serialization` is missing.

As a result, Mypy, Pyright, and Pyrefly reject valid calls that succeed at runtime.

All three calls in the example below succeed at runtime.

Mypy currently reports errors equivalent to:

```text
Argument "context" to "model_dump" of "RootModel" has incompatible type "str"
Unexpected keyword argument "fallback" for "model_dump" of "RootModel"
Unexpected keyword argument "polymorphic_serialization" for "model_dump" of "RootModel"
```

Pyright and Pyrefly report the same signature incompatibilities.

## Expected behavior

The type-checking-only `RootModel.model_dump()` declaration should accept the same parameters, annotations, defaults, and ordering as `BaseModel.model_dump()`, while preserving the more precise `RootModel` return annotation.

## Cause

The declaration appears to have drifted as the base method evolved:

- Serialization context originally updated both signatures.
- `BaseModel.context` was later widened to `Any`.
- `fallback` was subsequently added to `BaseModel.model_dump()`.
- `polymorphic_serialization` was later added to `BaseModel.model_dump()`.

Those later changes were not propagated to the manually maintained `RootModel` declaration.

## Proposed fix

Update only the static `RootModel.model_dump()` signature and add focused regression cases to `tests/typechecking/root_model.py`.

No runtime serialization behavior needs to change.

I have prepared and locally validated a focused two-file fix. The following checks pass:

- Mypy type-checking suite
- Pyright type-checking suite
- Pyrefly type-checking suite
- Focused RootModel serialization tests
- Ruff lint and formatting checks
- `git diff --check`

I would be happy to submit the PR after the issue is reviewed and assigned.

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, RootModel, SerializationInfo, model_serializer


class ContextRoot(RootModel[str]):
    @model_serializer
    def serialize_root(self, info: SerializationInfo) -> str:
        return f'{info.context}:{self.root}'


class Unknown:
    pass


class Base(BaseModel):
    x: int


class Sub(Base):
    y: int


ContextRoot(root='value').model_dump(context='prefix')

RootModel[Any](root=Unknown()).model_dump(
    mode='json',
    fallback=lambda _: 'fallback',
)

RootModel[list[Base]](root=[Sub(x=1, y=2)]).model_dump(
    polymorphic_serialization=True,
)
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text

        pydantic-core version: 2.47.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=debug pgo=false
               python version: 3.13.5 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Jun 12 2025, 11:23:37) [Clang 14.0.6 ]
                     platform: macOS-15.7.3-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O
             related packages: mypy-1.18.2 typing_extensions-4.15.0 pydantic-settings-2.7.1 pyright-1.1.407
                       commit: b281d5aed
```

title: Unexpected serialization schema with `ValidateAs`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way. Each keeps the `from_type` schema for validation and attaches a wrap serializer, `lambda v, h: h(v)`, built on the core schema of the `source` type. With that change the issue's example (`int` validated via `list[int]`) serializes without the spurious warning.

Patch A handles more edges.
- It suppresses `ArbitraryTypeWarning` while probing the source schema, which avoids a likely new warning for arbitrary source types.
- It reuses an existing `serialization` key from the source schema when one is present.
- It falls back to the original behaviour for `is-instance` or ungeneratable source schemas.
- It fixes the JSON schema in serialization mode. A wrap serializer without a `return_schema` would otherwise make the serialization-mode JSON schema reflect `from_type` (`list[int]`) rather than `int`. Patch A adds a `pydantic_js_annotation_functions` hook to generate it from the source schema.

Patch B leaves that JSON schema discrepancy unaddressed. For arbitrary source types it falls back to `any_schema` serialization, which is reasonable. It catches the broader `GENERATE_SCHEMA_ERRORS`, but it does not guard against the arbitrary-type warning.

On tests, Patch A is much stronger. It checks that the warning is gone (`simplefilter('error')`), JSON output, validation- and serialization-mode JSON schemas, `date` serialization in JSON mode, arbitrary types with and without `arbitrary_types_allowed`, and model and list-of-model sources with `include`/`exclude` pass-through. Patch B's tests are minimal: one JSON dump check that would mostly pass even before the fix, since only a warning is emitted, and one arbitrary-type dump. Patch B also renames an existing test and adds an unrelated comment elsewhere, which is minor churn.

Patch A is more complex, but the extra handling is justified and well commented.

### Initial Checks

### Description

From https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/discussions/13232:

```python

judge.reasoning:
Both patches let `EllipsisType` validate `...` in Python mode, so both address the core ask. Patch B covers the issue's scenarios more completely; Patch A is the more principled core-level design but is functionally narrower.

Correctness and usefulness: Patch A adds a new Rust core schema with a validator, serializer and error type, but stops short in several places.
- Its validator only accepts Python input (`input.as_python()`), so any JSON validation always fails.
- `dump_json` always errors.
- JSON schema generation raises.
- It only maps `EllipsisType`, not `...` used as a type, e.g. `Union[int, ...]`, which is closest to what the issue's `int | Ellipsis` example tries to express.
- So a model like the issue's `tuple[int | EllipsisType, int | EllipsisType]` validates in Python but cannot be dumped to JSON or validated from JSON.

Patch B builds the schema from existing core primitives and handles more cases.
- It uses `json_or_python_schema`, with `literal_schema([...])` for Python and the `'...'` string for JSON.
- It adds a JSON-mode plain serializer that warns on unexpected values.
- It maps both `Ellipsis` and `EllipsisType`, so `Union[int, ...]` works.
- The result is full round-tripping and a sensible JSON schema (`const: '...'`). Representing `...` as `'...'` in JSON is opinionated but documented and consistent.

Risk: Patch A touches Rust validator/serializer enums, error types and the core_schema API, which is a large surface for limited capability. Patch B is self-contained in `_generate_schema.py`. One small risk in B is that mapping `...` itself could intercept other uses of `...`. However, contexts like `tuple[int, ...]` and `Callable[..., X]` are handled before this mapping is reached.

Tests: Patch B's tests are substantive.
- Models with list and dict containers.
- Python and JSON round-trips and the expected JSON schema.
- Error types and locations.
- Unions including `Union[int, ...]` and `Optional`.
- Serialization of other union members and the unexpected-value warning.
- The issue's tuple subset scenario.

Patch A's tests are thinner: an error-list entry, a schema-function entry, one test asserting the JSON schema raises, and a small `TypeAdapter` test.

Overall, Patch B fixes more of what users of the issue need and verifies it better.

### Initial Checks

### Description

`Ellipsis` is a builtin type that `pydantic` does not support. Its usage is infrequent, but it can be useful to express placeholders:

This is a bit of a contrived example, but:
```python
class Model(pydantic.BaseModel):
    m: list[list[float]]
    subset: tuple[int | Ellipsis, int | Ellipsis]

    def subset_arr(self) -> np.NDArray:
        return np.asarray(self.m)[*self.subset]
```

Here's how I implement this right now with an adapter: https://github.com/psalvaggio/scientific_pydantic/blob/main/src/scientific_pydantic/ellipsis.py

However, since this is a standard library type, I think this would be a good thing to live in `pydantic` itself.

+

+
+#[derive(Debug)]
+pub struct EllipsisSerializer {}
+

+    LazyLock::new(|| Arc::new(EllipsisSerializer {}.into()));

+    const EXPECTED_TYPE: &'static str = "ellipsis";
+
+    fn build(
+        _schema: &Bound<'_, PyDict>,
+        _config: Option<&Bound<'_, PyDict>>,
+        _definitions: &mut DefinitionsBuilder<Arc<CombinedSerializer>>,
+    ) -> PyResult<Arc<CombinedSerializer>> {
+        Ok(ELLIPSIS_SERIALIZER.clone())
+    }
+}
+
+impl_py_gc_traverse!(EllipsisSerializer {});
+
+impl TypeSerializer for EllipsisSerializer {
+    fn to_python(&self, value: &Bound<'_, PyAny>, _state: &mut SerializationState<'_>) -> PyResult<Py<PyAny>> {
+        let ellipsis = PyEllipsis::get(value.py());
+
+        if value.is(ellipsis) {
+            Ok(ellipsis.to_owned().into_any().unbind())
+        } else {
+            Err(
+                PydanticSerializationUnexpectedValue::new_from_msg(Some("Expected 'Ellipsis' object".to_string()))
+                    .to_py_err(),
+            )
+        }
+    }
+
+    fn json_key<'a, 'py>(
+        &self,
+        key: &'a Bound<'py, PyAny>,
+        state: &mut SerializationState<'py>,

+    }

title: Allow arbitrary core schemas for serialization

judge.reasoning:
Patch B adds an explicit `SchemaSerSchema` (`{'type': 'schema', 'schema': ...}`) with a `schema_ser_schema()` constructor. In Rust it builds the inner schema with `Self::build`, so nested `serialization` keys and definition refs are still honored. Because the new type is a distinct tag, it never collides with existing ser schema types. B then removes the identity-wrap-serializer workaround everywhere it appeared: ValidateAs, PlainValidator, InstanceOf, SkipValidation and the non-dict mapping case in `_generate_schema`. It also updates JSON schema generation to handle the new type. Its tests cover pydantic-core (list, typed dict, dataclass, definition refs, overriding the outer type, nested serialization, error on a missing inner schema) and pydantic itself (ValidateAs, InstanceOf, SkipValidation, PlainValidator, OrderedDict serialization, and the serialization JSON schema). Those tests check the real end-to-end behavior the issue asks for.

Patch A takes a more invasive route: any core schema can be used directly as a serialization schema. This is inherently ambiguous because `function-plain` and `function-wrap` validator schemas share type tags with the function ser schemas. Patch A acknowledges this and works around it with a Python-side `as_ser_schema` helper. It also reshapes `SerSchema` into a string-literal type alias and touches `IncEx*` aliases and `json_schema.py` (rewritten as a `match`) for typing reasons, which is churn and adds risk. Most importantly, Patch A does not remove any of the workarounds the issue points at. It only rewrites the TODO in ValidateAs, so pydantic still uses identity wrap serializers. Its tests are mostly pydantic-core-level plus a unit test for a helper that nothing uses yet.

Patch B is the more correct, less risky and more complete resolution, with stronger tests.

issue_md:
As per the TODO in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13487:

There is currently no way to tell `pydantic-core` "serialize this value using this core schema". `Ser`Schema is:

```python
SerSchema = Union[
    SimpleSerSchema,
    PlainSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    WrapSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    FormatSerSchema,
    ToStringSerSchema,
    ModelSerSchema,
]
```

The only member that expresses "use this schema" is `SimpleSerSchema`, and it does not take a schema at all, only a name from a closed literal:

```python
ExpectedSerializationTypes = Literal[
    'none', 'int', 'bool', 'float', 'str', 'bytes', 'bytearray', 'list', 'tuple',
    'set', 'frozenset', 'generator', 'dict', 'datetime', 'date', 'time', 'timedelta',
    'url', 'multi-host-url', 'json', 'uuid', 'any',
]

class SimpleSerSchema(TypedDict, total=False):
    type: Required[ExpectedSerializationTypes]
```

So an arbitrary schema (a model, a dataclass, `list[int]`, a TypedDict, anything constructed by the schema generator) cannot be used directly. Every place in Pydantic that needs it works around the gap the same way: it wraps the schema in a wrap serializer whose function is the identity, purely so the schema can ride along in the `schema` argument.

From `ValidateAs.__get_pydantic_core_schema__()`:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/27f95c789b20aa23306e5ce559327db0e9a10a6e/pydantic/functional_validators.py#L911-L917

+def as_ser_schema(schema: CoreSchema) -> core_schema.SerSchema:
+    """Return a schema suitable for the `'serialization'` key of a core schema, from an arbitrary core schema.
+
+    Any core schema can be used as a serialization schema, except `'function-plain'` and `'function-wrap'`
+    schemas, as these types are already used by the plain and wrap serializer *function* schemas.
+    For these, mimic what pydantic-core would do if they were used as the *main* schema:
+
+    - if the function schema has a `'serialization'` schema, use it.
+    - otherwise, a `'function-plain'` schema is serialized as `'any'`, and a `'function-wrap'` schema
+      is serialized using its inner schema.
+
+    Note that `schema` is expected to be a *core* schema (e.g. as returned by the schema generator),
+    not an existing `'serialization'` schema.
+    """
+    if schema['type'] == 'function-plain' or schema['type'] == 'function-wrap':
+        if (ser_schema := schema.get('serialization')) is not None:
+            return ser_schema
+        if schema['type'] == 'function-plain':
+            return core_schema.any_schema()
+        return as_ser_schema(schema['schema'])
+    return schema
+

title: model_dump(exclude=...) is silently ignored in python mode when a wrap model_serializer is gated with when_used="json"

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the bug at its root cause in the same way. In `function.rs`, the function serializer used to clear include/exclude unconditionally before delegating to the return or fallback serializer. Both patches now clear it only when the user function actually ran. When `when_used` skips the function, the caller's include/exclude reaches the fallback serializer. Patch A passes the existing `state` straight through. Patch B re-scopes with a clone of the current include/exclude via a new `include_exclude()` accessor. These behave the same, and both cover `to_python`, `json_key` and `serde_serialize`, so correctness is a wash. On craft, Patch B is tidier: it adds the include/exclude value to the match tuple and keeps a single call site. Patch A uses a `used` flag with two near-identical if/else branches, which is more verbose but clear and well commented. Tests are where they differ. Patch B adds one test covering plain and wrap model serializers with `when_used='json'`, checking python-mode exclude/include and JSON-mode output. Patch A adds core-level tests in `pydantic-core` and parametrizes over `json` and `json-unless-none`. It also checks `to_json` and `model_dump_json`, covers the plain-function fallback for `unless-none` and the nullable case, and covers nested models (including `__all__` list exclusion) and field-level wrap serializers. All of these would fail before the fix. That is a more thorough regression suite for the exact scenarios the issue raises, including the identity-handler wrap case from the report, which Patch B's test does not use. Tests outrank craft, so Patch A's stronger and more targeted tests outweigh Patch B's slightly cleaner implementation.

title: Cannot create `defauldict` field with `dict` value type

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause by adding `dict` (and `frozenset`) to the inferred default-factory mapping, so `defaultdict[str, dict]` works. Patch B does exactly that, minimally, inside the existing dict. Its tests would fail before the fix and pass after: they cover `dict`, `dict[str, int]`, `typing.Dict[str, int]`, `frozenset` and `frozenset[int]`, and check both the value and the exact type. It also adds a BaseModel test that reproduces the issue's example (`prop: defaultdict[str, dict] = defaultdict(dict)`). Patch A fixes the issue too, and it corrects the 'keys' → 'values' wording in the error message. But it adds a Python-3.15-only branch that silently remaps `collections.abc.Mapping` from `dict` to `frozendict`. That is an unrelated behavior change: on newer Pythons, existing users of `defaultdict[..., Mapping]` would get immutable defaults, which risks breaking code that mutates them. It also relies on an undeclared `frozendict` name with `noqa: F821`. Patch A rewrites the existing infer test into a parametrized version, which gives reasonable coverage, but it does not test parameterized `dict[...]` or the model scenario from the issue. On the narrow fix the two are equivalent. B wins because it avoids A's risky scope creep and its tests target the reported scenario more directly.

title: Memory leak: transient models using Enum methods or Field(exclude_if=...) survive GC

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the three root-cause edges the issue names: `serialization_exclude_if` in `SerField`, `class` in `EnumSerializer`, and `lookup` in every `EnumValidator<T>`. On the core fix they are equivalent.

Patch B also traverses `serialization_exclude_if` on `ComputedField`. That is the same bug pattern, reachable via `@computed_field(exclude_if=...)`. B likewise traverses the previously skipped `expected_py_values` and `expected_py_primitives` in `LiteralLookup`. These are small, mechanical, low-risk additions in the spirit of the issue. They do not obscure the main fix.

Tests favour B:
- B adds pydantic-core GC tests for the enum validator and serializer, parametrized. The enum in these tests has a method, matching the issue.
- B adds tests for exclude_if on both fields and computed fields, and for unhashable literals.
- B adds an end-to-end test in `tests/test_main.py` that reproduces the issue's transient-module scenario through real `BaseModel`.
- B keeps the existing free-threaded xfail markers.

Patch A's new tests are reasonable, but A also churns the existing tests without reason:
- It deletes the `is_free_threaded` xfail markers from `test_gc_schema_serializer` and `test_gc_schema_validator`. This could cause new failures on free-threaded Python before 3.14.
- It renames `__schema__` and `__validator__` attributes.
- It turns comments into docstrings and drops imports.

This churn adds risk and obscures the fix. B gives equal core correctness with broader coverage of the same bug class, stronger regression tests including an issue-level repro, and no risky edits to existing tests.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Transient `BaseModel` classes are not collected when either:
* A model field references an `Enum` whose class defines a Python method.
* A model field uses `Field(exclude_if=<Python callable>)`.

After the defining module is removed from `sys.modules` and every ordinary strong reference is dropped, weak references to the model and enum classes remain alive after repeated full `gc.collect()` calls. Repeating this construction in disposable module namespaces causes linear memory growth.

Controls using an enum without methods or a field without `exclude_if` are collected normally.

I encountered this in combination with a Temporal workflow sandbox. With a large interconnected model graph and high volume Temporal workflows this can result in multi-GiB process growth relatively quickly.

The likely cause is missing `PyGcTraverse` edges for Python objects held by pydantic-core:
* `SerField` owns `serialization_exclude_if`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/fields.rs#L26-L38
* `EnumSerializer` owns `class`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/type_serializers/enum_.rs
* Each `EnumValidator<T>` owns `lookup`, but traverses only `class` and `missing`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/validators/enum_.rs

Traversing `py_schema` does not compensate for another unreported direct reference: CPython’s collector accounts for every actual strong edge individually.

I tested a temporary build from Pydantic `main` at `c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c`. Adding only these traversal edges made all objects in the reproduction collectible:
* Add `serialization_exclude_if` to `SerField` traversal.
* Add `class` to `EnumSerializer` traversal.
* Add `lookup` to every `EnumValidator<T>` traversal.

For the enum case, changing only the serializer or only the validator was insufficient; both missing edges were required.

This appears related to earlier missing-traversal fixes such as:

* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/5136
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/787
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1100

I would be happy to submit a focused patch.

(please note that this analysis was LLM assisted)

### Example Code

```Python
import gc
import sys
import types
import weakref

def transient_module(name, source, class_names):
    module = types.ModuleType(name)
    sys.modules[name] = module
    exec(compile(source, f"<{name}>", "exec"), module.__dict__)
    refs = tuple(
        weakref.ref(module.__dict__[class_name])
        for class_name in class_names
    )
    del sys.modules[name]
    del module
    return refs

enum_ref, enum_model_ref = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_enum_gc_repro",
    """
from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Membership(str, Enum):
    FULL = "full"
    def label(self) -> str:
        return self.value
class Model(BaseModel):
    membership: Membership
""",
    ("Membership", "Model"),
)

(exclude_if_model_ref,) = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_exclude_if_gc_repro",
    """
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class Model(BaseModel):
    value: int = Field(exclude_if=lambda value: False)
""",
    ("Model",),
)

for _ in range(5):
    gc.collect()

# All three should be False because no intentional strong references remain.
print("enum alive:", enum_ref() is not None)
print("enum model alive:", enum_model_ref() is not None)
print("exclude_if model alive:", exclude_if_model_ref() is not None)

title: TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' in match_type for PEP 695 aliases with a ParamSpec (regression in 2.14.0b1)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches stop the crash at `match_type`, but B is the safer, more complete, and better-tested fix.

Correctness: Patch A swaps the lookup to `typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES_IDS.get(id(obj))`. Deprecated aliases such as `typing.List` are singletons, so an identity lookup is sound in principle and avoids hashing. However, the fix depends on an attribute that only exists in a newer typing-inspection, which A handles by bumping the minimum to >=0.4.4. That attribute cannot be verified from the diff. The bump also widens the change's blast radius: if the attribute or version is wrong, every `match_type` call breaks. Patch B wraps the existing `.get(obj)` in `try/except TypeError`, which is self-contained and directly implements the issue's suggestion; an unhashable object can never be a key, so skipping it is correct. B also guards the `json_encoders.get(base)` lookup in `_add_custom_serialization_from_json_encoders`. The same unhashable `Alias[[], int]` would raise there when `json_encoders` is configured, so this is a real latent crash on the issue's scenario, not unrelated churn.

Tests: B's tests reproduce the reported case exactly: a `TypeAliasType` with a `ParamSpec`, parameterized with `[]` and `[int, str]`, inside a `BaseModel` with `| None`. They also exercise `TypeAdapter` and the json_encoders path. All of these would fail before the fix. A's test (`test_unhasbable_generic_alias`, which is also misspelled) uses `list[Annotated[int, Meta()]]` with unhashable metadata. That is the same mechanism but not the reported ParamSpec scenario.

Scope and craft: A adds a dependency floor bump, which carries upgrade risk. B's changes are local, commented, and consistent with the surrounding code. B is more verbose, but its control flow is clear.

issue_md:
Reported downstream in Giskard-AI/giskard#2719 (breaks `import giskard.checks`); repro and analysis below. The report was drafted jointly with @davidberenstein1957, who invited it to be filed upstream as-is.

### Description

`_generate_schema.match_type` added an unguarded dict lookup in 2.14 that assumes the annotation object is hashable. It is not, for a PEP 695 type alias with a `ParamSpec` parameterized by an empty list. Schema building for any model containing such an annotation crashes.

This is a regression: the same code builds fine on 2.13.4.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel

type Alias[**P, R] = Any

class M(BaseModel):
    f: Alias[[], int] | None = None
```

Raises immediately at class-definition time:

```
File ".../pydantic/_internal/_generate_schema.py", line 1127, in match_type
    if origin is not None and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
```

### Mechanism

`Alias[[], int]` is a `types.GenericAlias` whose `__args__` is `([], int)`. Hashing the alias hashes that tuple, which contains a `list` — so it is unhashable. The line at `_generate_schema.py:1127`

```python
if origin is not None and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
```

calls `.get(obj)` without checking that `obj` can be hashed. `dict.get` propagates the `TypeError` rather than treating an unhashable key as absent.

### Suggested fix

Guard the lookup, e.g.

```python
if origin is not None and isinstance(obj, Hashable) and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
```

or wrap it in `try/except TypeError`. An unhashable object cannot be a `DEPRECATED_ALIASES` key by construction, so skipping the lookup is always correct.

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

- pydantic 2.14.0b1 (fails) / 2.13.4 (works)
- Python 3.12.13
- Reproduced on Linux and macOS

### Real-world impact

Hit in [giskard-oss](https://github.com/Giskard-AI/giskard-oss), where `type GeneratorType[**P, R, S] = ...` parameterized as `GeneratorType[[], InputType, None]` makes `import giskard.checks` fail outright under 2.14.0b1. Instrumenting `match_type` confirms the offending object:

```
OFFENDING obj  = GeneratorType[[], InputType, None]
OFFENDING type = <class 'types.GenericAlias'>
OFFENDING args = ([], InputType, None)
```

There is no workaround on the library side short of pinning `pydantic<2.14` (done in Giskard-AI/giskard#2752), which is what downstream has had to do.

title: `SerializeAsAny` fails on a deferred model: `TypeError: 'MockValSer' object is not an instance of 'SchemaSerializer'`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause in `get_pydantic_serializer`. When the downcast fails, each calls the mock's `rebuild()` and uses the serializer it returns. Both also route `serialize_pydantic_serializable` through that helper, so the `SerializeAsAny` path and the polymorphism trampoline are both covered.

The key correctness difference is namespace resolution during the rebuild. Patch A calls `rebuild()` with its default `_parent_namespace_depth=5`. When the call comes from Rust deep inside serialization, frame 5 is an unrelated caller frame. Forward references could then resolve against whatever namespace happens to sit there, either succeeding wrongly or failing unpredictably. Patch B adds a `parent_namespace_depth` parameter through `MockValSer.rebuild` and the `attempt_rebuild` handlers, and passes 0 from Rust. Its test `test_serialization_inference_unbuildable_model` checks that a caller-local `Undefined = int` does not leak into the rebuild. `test_serialization_inference_rebuilds_incomplete_model` checks that module-level forward refs still resolve.

Error handling in the trampoline also favours B. B makes the helper return `Option`, so only a missing attribute (stdlib dataclasses) falls back, and real rebuild errors propagate. Patch A pattern-matches `AttributeError`/`TypeError` to decide when to fall back. That fallback could silently hide a `TypeError` raised during a rebuild and quietly serialize with the parent-class serializer.

On tests, A has the more thorough coverage of the exact issue scenario: annotation, flag and polymorphic paths, in both python and json modes, plus rebuild-failure cases. B covers the flag and polymorphic paths, plus the namespace-correctness cases. Both sets would fail before their fix.

On scope, B carries extra churn: moving `py_get_attrs` into `tools.rs` and an unrelated xfail test in `test_construction.py`. That is mostly neutral. B's handling of the frame-namespace hazard makes it the more robust fix overall.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Serialization with `SerializeAsAny` fails when the runtime class of the value is a deferred model.
A deferred model is a model with `defer_build=True` that pydantic did not build yet.
The call raises this error:

```
PydanticSerializationError: Error serializing to JSON: TypeError: 'MockValSer' object is not an instance of 'SchemaSerializer'
```

I expect pydantic to build the deferred model at first use, and then serialize the value.

### Cause

The cause is in pydantic-core, in `src/serializers/infer.rs`.
The function `serialize_pydantic_serializable` reads the attribute `__pydantic_serializer__` from the value.
On a deferred model, this attribute holds a `MockValSer` object, not a `SchemaSerializer` object.
The code downcasts the object to `SchemaSerializer`.
The downcast fails, and the error goes to the caller.

`MockValSer` has a lazy rebuild hook in `__getattr__`.
A Python method call starts this hook.
A Rust downcast does not start this hook.
As a result, the same deferred instance serializes correctly through a direct `model_dump_json()`, but fails through `SerializeAsAny`.
The example code below shows this asymmetry.

### Impact

This failure occurred for us in production.
A worker process serialized instances of model classes that it never validated in that process.
Each `model_dump_json()` call on the parent model failed.

### Versions tested

The failure occurs on all versions that we tested:

- pydantic 2.12.5 / pydantic-core 2.41.5
- pydantic 2.13.4 / pydantic-core 2.46.4
- pydantic 2.14.0b1 / pydantic-core 2.48.0

### Related issues

- #7713 tracks `MockValSer` errors in general.
- #12282 reported this failure and was closed as a duplicate.

### Proposed fix

I have a fix with tests ready on a fork.
The fix changes `get_pydantic_serializer` in `infer.rs`:

1. The function downcasts the attribute value to `SchemaSerializer` as before.
2. If the downcast fails, the function calls the `rebuild()` method of the mock object.
3. The function then uses the serializer that `rebuild()` returns.
4. An object without a `rebuild()` method keeps the current downcast error.

`serialize_pydantic_serializable` and `PolymorphismTrampoline` use the same code path, so one change repairs both.
All pydantic and pydantic-core test suites pass with the fix.
Please assign this issue to me, and I will open the pull request.


### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Optional

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, SerializeAsAny


class Child(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(defer_build=True)
    x: int = 1


class Sub(Child):
    y: int = 2


class Parent(BaseModel):
    content: Optional[SerializeAsAny[Child]] = None


# model_construct() does not validate, so pydantic does not build Sub.
# This is equal to a process that serializes a class that it never validated.
sub = Sub.model_construct(x=1, y=2)
parent = Parent.model_construct(content=sub)
assert Sub.__pydantic_complete__ is False

# 1) The SerializeAsAny path fails on the deferred model.
try:
    parent.model_dump_json()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    # PydanticSerializationError: Error serializing to JSON: TypeError:
    # 'MockValSer' object is not an instance of 'SchemaSerializer'

# 2) The direct Python path rebuilds the same deferred model and succeeds.
print(sub.model_dump_json())  # {"x":1,"y":2}
assert Sub.__pydantic_complete__ is True

# 3) After the rebuild, the SerializeAsAny path also succeeds.
print(parent.model_dump_json())  # {"content":{"x":1,"y":2}}
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.14.0b1
        pydantic-core version: 2.48.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.11.15 (main, Mar 25 2026, 02:58:47) [Clang 22.1.1 ]
                     platform: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.16.0
                       commit: unknown

The same example also fails on these versions:
- pydantic 2.13.4 / pydantic-core 2.46.4 (latest stable)
- pydantic 2.12.5 / pydantic-core 2.41.5
```

title: Runtime by_name/by_alias arguments dropped by model_validator(mode="wrap")

judge.reasoning:
The Rust changes in generator.rs are functionally identical. Both add `by_alias`/`by_name` fields to `InternalValidator`, capture them from `extra` in `new()`, and forward them in both `validate()` and `validate_assignment()` instead of hardcoding `None`. This fixes the root cause: the wrap-validator handler (and the generator item validator) built a fresh `Extra` that dropped the runtime settings. Field placement differs slightly, which is immaterial, so correctness is a tie.

The difference is in testing.

Patch A's tests cover every path its change touches:
- **Wrap handler, core level:** `validate_python`, `validate_json` and `validate_strings` through a wrap validator, compared directly against an unwrapped validator.
- **Assignment path:** `validate_assignment` through a wrap handler, which exercises the second modified method.
- **Generator path:** the `InternalValidator` used for lazy generator items.
- **Issue repro:** the exact pydantic-level scenario from the issue (alias_generator, `TypeAdapter.validate_python`, `model_validate_json`), comparing Plain vs Wrapped across three by_alias/by_name combinations.

All of these would fail before the fix.

Patch B's tests are narrower:
- **First test:** checks a wrap model validator and a nested wrap field validator with `model_validate`. This would fail before the fix and is relevant.
- **Second test:** covers strict/extra/from_attributes/context forwarding. These were already forwarded before the patch, so it adds no regression value for this issue.
- **Gaps:** nothing covers JSON validation, the `validate_assignment` code path, or the generator path, even though the patch modifies them.

Scope and craft are comparable. Patch A wins on test coverage of the changed behavior.

title: JSON Schema ignores `ser_json_temporal`, so serialization schemas contradict `model_dump_json()` output

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the core schema bug the same way. `date_schema`, `time_schema` and `datetime_schema` now return `{'type': 'number'}` for 'seconds'/'milliseconds'. `timedelta_schema` mirrors pydantic-core's precedence by checking `'ser_json_temporal' in config_dict` before falling back to `ser_json_timedelta`. Both handle the issue's two scenarios: numeric temporal modes, and iso8601 temporal overriding float timedelta.

The difference is in default values. Patch A leaves `encode_default` calling `to_jsonable_python` with only `timedelta_mode`. With `ser_json_temporal='seconds'` and a datetime or timedelta default, A emits a schema that says `type: number` but carries an ISO-string `default`. That is internally contradictory and is the same 'schema disagrees with serialized output' problem the issue reports. Patch B passes `temporal_mode=config.ser_json_temporal` there too. Its parametrized dataclass and TypedDict tests confirm defaults become 1577836800.0 / 300.0 (and the millisecond equivalents).

One risk in B: I could not confirm from the diff alone how pydantic-core resolves `timedelta_mode` against an always-supplied `temporal_mode` when only `ser_json_timedelta='float'` is configured. If core does not apply the same precedence there, existing timedelta-default behavior could change. I judge this low risk because core explicitly supports both arguments, but it does limit my confidence somewhat.

On tests, both suites would fail before the fix and pass after. Each checks schema types against actual `model_dump_json` output and covers precedence. B goes further: it asserts the exact dumped values in the precedence cases, checks that a nested model with its own config gets the right schema in `$defs`, and covers defaults.

On craft, A's shared `_common_temporal_schema` helper is somewhat tidier than B's repeated inline checks, but that is minor.

Overall, B resolves the inconsistency more completely and has stronger tests.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`ser_json_temporal` landed in v2.12 and controls how `datetime`, `date`, `time` and `timedelta` are serialized to JSON. `GenerateJsonSchema` was never told about it, so a `mode='serialization'` schema still says these fields are strings even when `model_dump_json()` writes numbers.

With `ser_json_temporal='seconds'` (same with `'milliseconds'`), every temporal field is affected:

```
schema:  {'dt': {'type': 'string', 'format': 'date-time'}, 'td': {'type': 'string', 'format': 'duration'}}
dump:    {'dt': 1577836800.0, 'td': 86400.0}
```

Running that payload through a JSON Schema validator fails with `1577836800.0 is not of type 'string'`, so the schema pydantic publishes rejects the output pydantic itself just produced. `date_schema`, `time_schema` and `datetime_schema` read no config at all right now.

There is a second mismatch that goes the other way, on `timedelta`. `timedelta_schema` only looks at the older `ser_json_timedelta` setting. The docs for `ser_json_temporal` say it takes precedence over `ser_json_timedelta`, and pydantic-core implements exactly that: `SerializationConfig::from_config` and `TimeDeltaSerializer::build` both check whether `ser_json_temporal` is present in the config before falling back to `ser_json_timedelta`. The JSON schema layer does not, so setting `ser_json_temporal='iso8601'` together with `ser_json_timedelta='float'` gives you the reverse problem:

```
schema:  {'td': {'type': 'number'}}
dump:    {'td': 'P1D'}
```

For anyone generating an OpenAPI document from a model this is a silent wrong answer rather than a crash, which is probably why it has gone unnoticed since the setting was added.

I have a patch that mirrors the pydantic-core resolution in the four temporal schema methods, plus tests. Happy to open a PR if you want to assign this to me.

### Example Code

```Python
import json
from datetime import date, datetime, time, timedelta

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class Numeric(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(ser_json_temporal='seconds')

    dt: datetime
    d: date
    t: time
    td: timedelta


model = Numeric(dt=datetime(2020, 1, 1), d=date(2020, 1, 1), t=time(12, 0), td=timedelta(days=1))

print(Numeric.model_json_schema(mode='serialization')['properties'])
#> {'dt': {'format': 'date-time', 'title': 'Dt', 'type': 'string'},
#>  'd': {'format': 'date', 'title': 'D', 'type': 'string'},
#>  't': {'format': 'time', 'title': 'T', 'type': 'string'},
#>  'td': {'format': 'duration', 'title': 'Td', 'type': 'string'}}

print(json.loads(model.model_dump_json()))
#> {'dt': 1577836800.0, 'd': 1577836800.0, 't': 43200.0, 'td': 86400.0}


# The timedelta precedence case, wrong in the opposite direction:
class Precedence(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(ser_json_temporal='iso8601', ser_json_timedelta='float')

    td: timedelta


print(Precedence.model_json_schema(mode='serialization')['properties'])
#> {'td': {'title': 'Td', 'type': 'number'}}

print(json.loads(Precedence(td=timedelta(days=1)).model_dump_json()))
#> {'td': 'P1D'}
```

title: `populate_by_name` (and implicit `validate_by_name` when `validate_by_alias=False`) is ignored by `@validate_call`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause. The bug is that the arguments schemas embed the raw `validate_by_name` value, which overrides the core config.

Patch A adds `ConfigWrapper.resolved_validate_by_name()`. It resolves an explicit `validate_by_name` first, then falls back to `populate_by_name`, and finally treats `validate_by_alias is False` as enabling name validation. It uses this in both `_arguments_schema` and `_arguments_v3_schema`. That handles both scenarios in the issue: `populate_by_name=True` and the 'worse variant' with `validate_by_alias=False`. A also applies the resolved value to the generated `__init__` signatures for models and dataclasses. That is adjacent and low-risk, and it keeps signatures consistent with validation behavior. The main weakness is that the logic duplicates what `core_config()` already does, so the two could drift apart; the docstring at least says so.

Patch B calls `core_config(title=None)` and embeds `core_config.get('validate_by_name')`. This reuses the existing patching logic as a single source of truth, which is clean. If that patching also covers the `validate_by_alias=False` case, B fixes both scenarios too, and an unset value passes through as None so pydantic-core falls back to its config. It does build a whole core config just to read one key, which is a little wasteful.

The deciding factor is the tests. A tests both issue scenarios for `@validate_call` and for both experimental schema types. It checks that the alias still works under `populate_by_name`, and that under `validate_by_alias=False` the name works and the alias is rejected with specific error types. B only tests the `populate_by_name` name path, only for `arguments-v3` plus one `validate_call` case. It never exercises the `validate_by_alias=False` variant the issue calls worse. B also adds unrelated test churn (rewriting `dict(...)` as `{...}` in existing tests) and leaves placeholder `"""<link>"""` docstrings.

Correctness is roughly equal, so A wins on test coverage of the reported scenarios and on cleaner scope in its tests.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Since v2.11, `@validate_call(config=ConfigDict(populate_by_name=True))` no longer allows passing an aliased parameter by its name — the same config on a `BaseModel` works, and the [`populate_by_name` docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/config/#pydantic.config.ConfigDict.populate_by_name) say it is strictly equivalent to `validate_by_name=True, validate_by_alias=True` (deprecated in v3, but still supported). Works on 2.10.6; broken on 2.11.x, 2.12.x, and `main`.

A worse variant: `@validate_call(config=ConfigDict(validate_by_alias=False))` makes the aliased parameter impossible to provide at all (both name and alias raise), even though #11503 made `validate_by_alias=False` implicitly enable `validate_by_name`.

Root cause: `_arguments_schema()`/`_arguments_v3_schema()` embed `validate_by_name=self._config_wrapper.validate_by_name` into the core schema (`_generate_schema.py:2081/2149`), reading the raw config key. The backwards-compatibility patch mapping `populate_by_name` → `validate_by_name` only runs inside `ConfigWrapper.core_config()`, and pydantic-core gives the schema-embedded value precedence over the validator config, so the patched core config is never consulted. Models are unaffected because model-fields schemas don't embed the flag.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field, validate_call

@validate_call(config=dict(populate_by_name=True))
def f(a: Annotated[int, Field(alias='b')]) -> int:
    return a

f(b=1)  # OK
f(a=1)  # ValidationError: Unexpected keyword argument
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```text
             pydantic version: 2.14.0b1
        pydantic-core version: 2.48.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.11.14 (main, Oct  9 2025, 16:16:55) [Clang 17.0.0 (clang-1700.4.4.1)]
                     platform: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.16.0
                       commit: 2151025
```

(also reproduced on released pydantic 2.11.10 and 2.12.5; not reproducible on 2.10.6)
